title: PMP® Exam Prep
blurb: Instructor-led PMP preparation covering the full ECO — people, process, business environment — with practice exams and a pass-or-retrain-free guarantee. Taught by a PMP-certified practitioner.

modules.t: The Exam, the ECO & the PMI Mindset
modules.d: How the PMP is built, how it is scored, and the decision logic behind every correct answer.
modules.body:
What you are actually preparing for

The PMP is not a knowledge test. It is a judgment test. Almost every question puts you inside a realistic project situation — a sponsor changing priorities, a team member missing deadlines, a vendor slipping — and asks what an experienced, ethical project manager would do. Several answers will be things a reasonable person might do. Only one is what PMI considers the best professional response at this moment. Candidates who memorise definitions and formulas routinely fail; candidates who internalise the decision logic pass, often comfortably.

The exam is built from PMI's Examination Content Outline (ECO), not directly from the PMBOK® Guide. The ECO organises the exam into three domains — People, Process and Business Environment — each broken into tasks and enablers. The PMBOK® Guide, the Agile Practice Guide and Process Groups: A Practice Guide are reference sources, but the ECO defines what is tested and in what proportion. Roughly half of the questions reflect predictive (plan-driven) delivery and half reflect agile or hybrid approaches, distributed across all three domains rather than isolated in an "agile section".

Verify before you book. PMI periodically revises the ECO, the question count, timing and domain weights. Before scheduling, download the current ECO and the PMP Handbook from pmi.org and treat them as the authority. This course teaches the durable reasoning that survives every revision; your study plan should be calibrated to the current published weights.

Eligibility, application and audit

You need 35 contact hours of project management education (this programme provides them) plus documented experience leading projects: typically 36 months within the last eight years if you hold a four-year degree, or 60 months with a secondary-school diploma. Experience is described per project — objective, your role, and what you did across initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and closing. Write descriptions in PMI's vocabulary, in the first person, with outcomes. Applications are randomly selected for audit; if selected you must produce signed verification from supervisors and copies of education certificates before you can sit the exam. Keep those contacts warm before you apply.

How the exam behaves

Questions are mostly single-best-answer multiple choice, but you will also meet multiple response ("choose two"), matching, hotspot and occasional fill-in-the-blank calculation items. A share of questions are unscored pre-test items you cannot identify, so treat every question as live. There is no published pass mark: PMI uses psychometric analysis and reports performance per domain as Above Target, Target, Below Target or Needs Improvement. The practical implication is that you cannot "bank" one strong domain to rescue a weak one — your plan must lift every domain.

The PMI mindset — the decision logic behind correct answers

When two or three answers look defensible, these principles break the tie. They are not tricks; they describe how a mature project leader behaves.

  • Assess before you act. When something new happens — a risk triggers, a conflict surfaces, a change is requested — the best first move is usually to understand it: review the relevant plan or log, gather facts, analyse impact. Jumping straight to a fix, an escalation or a decision is usually premature.
  • Use the process that already exists. Changes go through integrated change control. Risks go to the risk register and its owners. Issues go to the issue log. Answers that bypass agreed processes — even with good intent — are almost always wrong.
  • Handle it at the lowest appropriate level first. Talk privately with the team member before involving their functional manager. Work the problem with the team before going to the sponsor. Escalate when something is outside your authority or tolerance, not as a first reflex.
  • Be a servant leader. In agile and hybrid contexts especially, the PM removes impediments, coaches, facilitates and protects the team; they do not assign tasks inside a self-organising team or override its estimates.
  • Be proactive and root-cause oriented. Prefer answers that prevent recurrence over answers that only treat the symptom.
  • Deliver value, not just outputs. The project exists to enable benefits. Answers that protect business value and stakeholder outcomes beat answers that protect the plan for its own sake.
  • Act ethically, always. The PMI Code of Ethics — responsibility, respect, fairness, honesty — overrides convenience. Never hide information, never accept improper gifts, never misreport status.
A useful self-check on hard questions: "If my best mentor were watching me make this choice, would they nod — or would they ask why I skipped a step?"

Reading a question like an examiner

Train yourself to read the last sentence first — it tells you what is being asked: the first action, the next action, the best approach, or what the PM should have done. Then read the scenario hunting for three signals: the delivery approach (predictive, agile, hybrid — it changes the right answer), the stage of the project (a problem in initiating is handled differently from the same problem in closing), and what has already been done (if the scenario says the PM already analysed the impact, analysing it again is wrong; the next step is the decision process).

Words such as immediately, always and ignore often mark wrong answers. Answers that sound active but skip analysis ("Replace the team member", "Escalate to the sponsor", "Crash the schedule") are classic distractors. Answers that sound passive but are sometimes correct include "review the risk register" or "meet with the stakeholder to understand their concern" — because understanding precedes action.

Building your personal study plan

A proven rhythm for working professionals is eight to ten weeks at eight to twelve hours per week. Start with a diagnostic to find your weakest domain. Each week, learn one block of content, then immediately drill 40–60 situational questions on it, and — the step most candidates skip — review every question, including the ones you got right, writing down the principle that decided it. From week five onward, add a timed 60-question block weekly; in the last three weeks, sit at least two full-length timed mocks under exam conditions. Aim for consistent scores of 75–80% on quality question banks before booking.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a PMP exam coach. Ask me 8 diagnostic questions about my experience, schedule and confidence across the People, Process and Business Environment domains. Then build me a week-by-week 9-week study plan with weekly hours, topics, number of practice questions, mock-exam dates, and a readiness checkpoint each week.

📚 Glossary

  • ECO: Examination Content Outline — PMI's blueprint of domains, tasks and enablers that defines exam content.
  • Domain: one of the three major areas: People, Process, Business Environment.
  • Situational question: a scenario asking for the best, first or next action.
  • Pre-test item: an unscored question PMI is trialling, indistinguishable from scored items.
  • Contact hour: one hour of structured project management education.

📖 References

  • PMI, PMP Examination Content Outline (current edition, pmi.org).
  • PMI, PMP Certification Handbook.
  • PMI, Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct.
  • PMI, A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK® Guide); Agile Practice Guide.

quiz.q: A candidate argues the PMP should be studied primarily from the PMBOK® Guide because 'that is what the exam tests.' Which response best reflects how the exam is actually constructed?
opts: The exam is built from the ECO's domains and tasks; the PMBOK® Guide is one of several reference sources
The exam is built from the PMBOK® Guide but weighted by the ECO's domain percentages
The exam draws equally from PMBOK®, the Agile Practice Guide and the Code of Ethics by chapter
The exam is built from the PMBOK® Guide's process groups, with the ECO serving as a summary
quiz.x: PMI writes items against the ECO's domains, tasks and enablers. PMBOK® and the practice guides are references that inform answers, not the blueprint itself.

quiz.q: A team member tells you a key supplier has just announced a three-week delay on critical equipment. What should you do FIRST?
opts: Request approval from the sponsor to switch to the backup supplier
Assess the impact of the delay on the schedule, cost and dependent activities
Submit a change request to re-baseline the project schedule
Implement the risk response already listed in the risk register
quiz.x: New information is analysed before acting. Even a planned risk response should be checked against the actual impact first; switching suppliers or re-baselining are decisions that follow analysis.

quiz.q: During a hybrid project, a functional manager repeatedly pulls a developer off sprint work for operational tasks. The PM has already discussed it privately with the developer, who has no control over it. What is the BEST next step?
opts: Escalate the issue to the project sponsor for resolution
Remove the developer from the team and request a dedicated replacement
Log the issue and reduce the team's sprint commitments to absorb the loss
Meet with the functional manager to discuss resource commitments and agree a solution
quiz.x: The lowest appropriate level after the developer is the functional manager who controls the resource. Escalation to the sponsor comes only if that conversation fails.

quiz.q: Which statement about PMP scoring is MOST accurate?
opts: Agile questions are weighted more heavily than predictive questions in the final score
Pre-test items are identified on screen so candidates can skip them safely
Performance is reported by domain bands, and there is no published fixed pass percentage
Candidates need 61% correct overall, with a minimum of 50% in each domain
quiz.x: PMI reports Above Target / Target / Below Target / Needs Improvement per domain and uses psychometric methods rather than a published cut score. Pre-test items are not identified.

quiz.q: A question states: 'The PM has analysed the impact of the requested change and documented it.' Which answer is MOST likely correct for what happens next?
opts: Submit the change request to the change control board for a decision
Inform the team so they can begin planning the new work
Implement the change because its impact is now understood
Analyse the impact on quality and risk before proceeding
quiz.x: The scenario tells you analysis is complete, so repeating it is wrong. In integrated change control the next step after analysis is a formal decision — implementation only follows approval.

quiz.q: On an agile team, the product owner asks the PM to assign specific stories to specific developers to speed up the sprint. How should the PM respond?
opts: Assign only the high-priority stories and let the team choose the rest
Ask the scrum master to assign the stories on the PM's behalf
Assign the stories, since the product owner is accountable for value delivery
Explain that the team self-organises around work and facilitate a discussion with the team
quiz.x: Self-organising teams decide who does what. A servant leader facilitates rather than assigning tasks, while helping the product owner express priority through the backlog.

quiz.q: A vendor offers the PM an expensive gift during contract negotiations, saying it is 'customary in our culture'. What should the PM do?
opts: Accept the gift, since respecting cultural norms is part of the Code of Ethics
Politely decline and follow the organisation's policy on gifts
Accept the gift but disclose it in the next status report
Accept the gift and recuse yourself from the final vendor selection
quiz.x: Responsibility and fairness in the Code of Ethics require avoiding conflicts of interest. Organisational policy governs; cultural respect does not override it, and disclosure after accepting does not remove the conflict.

quiz.q: Which reading strategy BEST reduces errors on long situational questions?
opts: Choose the most comprehensive option because it covers the most possibilities
Eliminate any option containing technical terms you do not recognise
Read the final sentence first to identify whether it asks for the first, next or best action
Read the scenario twice before looking at any of the options
quiz.x: The final sentence defines the task. 'First' versus 'next' versus 'best' routinely changes which plausible option is correct.

quiz.q: A candidate scores 92% on Process practice sets but 58% on People. Why is it risky to book the exam now?
opts: Because People questions are always asked first and affect later item difficulty
Because People questions carry the highest individual point value
Because performance is reported by domain and weak domains are not offset in the way candidates assume
Because PMI requires at least 70% in every domain on practice exams before booking
quiz.x: Domain-level performance matters and there is no reliable way to bank one domain against another. The plan must lift every domain.

quiz.q: Which experience description is MOST appropriate for the PMP application?
opts: Assisted the PM with various project tasks over two years
Led a 9-person team to deliver a clinic records system; developed the schedule and risk register, managed change control, and closed the project 3% under budget
Worked on many projects using best practices and PMBOK® processes
Responsible for project success and stakeholder satisfaction across the organisation
quiz.x: Strong descriptions are first-person, specific, use PM vocabulary across the lifecycle, and state outcomes. Vague or assistant-level descriptions invite audit questions.

modules.t: People I — Leading & Building High-Performing Teams
modules.d: Servant leadership, team development, motivation, conflict and performance.
modules.body:
Why the People domain decides most results

The People domain covers how you lead, build, support and protect a team. It is the most judgment-heavy part of the exam because the "right" answer depends on reading people, context and timing. The ECO tasks include managing conflict, leading a team, supporting team performance, empowering team members, ensuring adequate training, building a team, addressing impediments, negotiating agreements, collaborating with stakeholders, building shared understanding, engaging virtual teams, defining ground rules, mentoring, and promoting performance through emotional intelligence.

Servant leadership in practice

Servant leadership inverts the command pyramid: the leader exists to make the team successful. In practice that means four recurring behaviours. Shield the team from interruptions and scope churn. Remove impediments they cannot remove themselves — access, approvals, missing information. Grow capability through coaching, pairing and training rather than doing the work for them. Create clarity about the vision, priorities and definition of done. On exam questions, the servant-leader answer is usually the one where the PM facilitates the team to solve a problem rather than solving it for them — unless the problem is an organisational impediment the team cannot touch, in which case the PM should act.

Team21 edge: servant leadership is the backbone of Team21's "How Shall We Now Lead?" philosophy. Candidates who already practise it find the People domain far more intuitive — the exam is rewarding the same instincts: humility, stewardship and service that produces results.

Team development: Tuckman and what the PM does at each stage

Bruce Tuckman's model remains the exam's default lens. Forming: people are polite, uncertain, dependent on the leader — the PM provides direction, introductions, roles and a team charter. Storming: friction over approaches and authority — the PM coaches, mediates and reinforces ground rules; this stage is normal, not failure. Norming: agreements form, trust grows — the PM steps back and supports. Performing: the team is interdependent and self-directed — the PM delegates and removes obstacles. Adjourning: work ends — recognise contributions and capture lessons. Teams can regress when membership or goals change, so adding a new member to a performing team often pushes it back toward storming.

The team charter and ground rules

A team charter records values, working agreements, communication norms, decision-making processes, and conflict-handling rules. Its power on the exam: when a dispute arises over "how we work", the first move is often to refer to the team charter or ground rules — and if none exist, to facilitate creating them. Agreements the team writes themselves are far more durable than rules imposed by the PM.

Conflict: sources and techniques

Most project conflict stems from schedules, priorities, and resources — personalities are a less common root cause than people assume. Conflict is not inherently bad; handled well it surfaces better ideas. The five classic techniques:

  • Collaborate / problem-solve — work together to find a solution that satisfies the underlying concerns. Produces lasting win-win; usually the best answer when time allows and the issue matters.
  • Compromise / reconcile — each side gives something up. Useful under time pressure or when parties have equal power; often lose-lose.
  • Smooth / accommodate — emphasise agreement, downplay differences. Preserves relationships temporarily; problem may return.
  • Force / direct — impose a solution. Appropriate in emergencies, safety or ethics issues; damages trust if overused.
  • Withdraw / avoid — postpone or step back. Useful for cooling off or when the issue is trivial; dangerous if the issue is real.

Exam pattern: the PM first encourages the people involved to resolve it themselves, then facilitates privately, and uses formal or forcing measures only when necessary. Conflicts are addressed privately and directly, never in front of the group.

Motivation and emotional intelligence

Expect questions that draw on classic theories. Herzberg: hygiene factors (pay, conditions, policy) prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate; motivators (achievement, recognition, growth, meaningful work) drive performance. McClelland: people are driven by achievement, affiliation or power to differing degrees — tailor recognition accordingly. Maslow: unmet basic needs crowd out higher motivation. Theory X/Y: assuming people need control (X) versus assuming they seek responsibility (Y) — modern PM practice leans Y. Emotional intelligence — self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship management — is how a PM applies all of this in the moment.

Underperformance: the escalation ladder

When a team member underperforms, the sequence matters. First, talk privately to understand why — skills, unclear expectations, personal circumstances, workload, or tooling. Then address the cause: training, mentoring, clarified expectations, reallocated workload. Document agreements. Involve the functional manager or HR only if the problem persists or exceeds your authority. Removing someone from the team is a last resort and rarely the first correct answer.

Virtual and distributed teams

Distributed teams need deliberate structure: overlap hours, agreed response times, a single source of truth for artefacts, video for relationship-building, explicit norms for asynchronous decisions, and attention to cultural differences in directness and hierarchy. A recurring exam scenario: a remote member is disengaged — the best response is a one-to-one conversation and adjusting the collaboration model, not a reprimand in the group channel.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a PMP People-domain simulator. Present me with 5 realistic team-conflict and underperformance scenarios from predictive, agile and hybrid projects. For each, give 4 plausible options. After I answer, explain the best choice using servant leadership, Tuckman stage and conflict-technique reasoning, and say what the PM should have done earlier to prevent it.

📚 Glossary

  • Servant leadership: leading by serving the team's needs so it can perform.
  • Team charter: the team's agreed values, norms and working rules.
  • Tuckman ladder: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning.
  • Hygiene factor: a factor whose absence causes dissatisfaction but whose presence does not motivate.
  • Impediment: anything blocking the team's progress that it cannot resolve alone.

📖 References

  • Tuckman, B. (1965). Developmental sequence in small groups. Psychological Bulletin.
  • Herzberg, F. (1968). One more time: how do you motivate employees? Harvard Business Review.
  • Greenleaf, R. K. (1977). Servant Leadership.
  • PMI, Agile Practice Guide.

quiz.q: Two senior engineers disagree openly in a team meeting about the system architecture, and the discussion is becoming heated. What should the PM do FIRST?
opts: Escalate the decision to the technical architect in the PMO
Ask the team to vote on the architecture so the decision is democratic
Decide the architecture based on the PM's own technical judgement to end the conflict
Ask the engineers to continue the discussion privately with the PM facilitating after the meeting
quiz.x: Conflict is handled privately and the PM first facilitates the parties toward collaborative problem-solving. Forcing, voting or escalation skip that step.

quiz.q: A high-performing team has just added two new members. Over the next week, disagreements about coding standards increase. What is the MOST likely explanation and response?
opts: The team has regressed toward storming; facilitate revisiting the working agreements together
The new members lack skill; arrange immediate training for them
The norming stage has failed; replace the new members
The team is adjourning; begin capturing lessons learned
quiz.x: Membership changes commonly push teams back to storming. Revisiting and co-owning working agreements helps the team re-norm.

quiz.q: A team member's work quality has dropped sharply over two weeks. What should the PM do FIRST?
opts: Raise the quality issue at the next retrospective so the team can address it
Meet privately with the team member to understand what has changed
Reassign their critical tasks to more reliable colleagues
Inform the team member's functional manager and request a performance review
quiz.x: Understanding the cause privately comes before reassigning work, escalating, or raising it publicly. The cause could be workload, skills, personal issues or unclear expectations.

quiz.q: Which leadership action BEST reflects servant leadership on an agile team?
opts: Assigning daily tasks so nobody is idle
Setting the sprint goal on behalf of the product owner
Securing access to a test environment the team has been waiting on for a week
Reviewing every pull request before it is merged
quiz.x: Removing organisational impediments the team cannot resolve is the core servant-leader contribution. Assigning tasks and setting goals for others undercut self-organisation and role boundaries.

quiz.q: A company has just raised salaries across the board, yet team engagement on the project remains low. According to Herzberg, what is the BEST next lever?
opts: Introduce stricter monitoring of individual productivity
Increase salaries further for the project team specifically
Improve office conditions and update HR policy
Give team members ownership of meaningful features and recognise their achievements
quiz.x: Pay and conditions are hygiene factors; they prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate. Achievement, recognition and responsibility are motivators.

quiz.q: A remote team member in another time zone has stopped contributing in team channels. What is the BEST response?
opts: Hold a one-to-one video call to understand the situation and adjust collaboration arrangements
Post a reminder in the team channel about participation expectations
Change all meetings to suit the remote member's hours
Request that the member be replaced with someone in the main time zone
quiz.x: Disengagement is first explored privately. Adjusting the collaboration model follows understanding; public reminders and replacement are premature, and a unilateral switch ignores the rest of the team.

quiz.q: Team members disagree about whether meetings should start late for colleagues who are commuting. There is a team charter. What should the PM do?
opts: Refer the team to the ground rules in the charter and, if needed, facilitate an update
Make a ruling so the team stops wasting time on the issue
Allow each member to decide for themselves to preserve autonomy
Ask the sponsor to set a company-wide policy
quiz.x: The charter exists for exactly this. Referring to it — and updating it together if it is silent — keeps ownership with the team.

quiz.q: During a safety-critical deployment, two team members argue about skipping a verification step to save time. Which conflict technique is MOST appropriate?
opts: Compromise by doing half of the verification step
Force the decision to perform the verification as required
Withdraw and let the team decide after the deployment
Smooth the disagreement to protect the relationship
quiz.x: Forcing is appropriate when safety, legal or ethical requirements are at stake. Compromise or avoidance here could cause harm.

quiz.q: A new team is in its first week. Members are polite, hesitant and keep asking the PM what to do next. What should the PM focus on?
opts: Stepping back to avoid creating dependency
Delegating fully so the team becomes self-directed quickly
Providing clear direction, roles, objectives and facilitating a team charter
Introducing healthy conflict to accelerate storming
quiz.x: This is forming. The team needs clarity, structure and introductions; delegation and stepping back fit later stages.

quiz.q: After coaching and clarified expectations, a team member's performance still has not improved and the deadline is at risk. What is the BEST next step?
opts: Complete the team member's work yourself to protect the deadline
Remove the team member from the project immediately
Ignore the issue until the project closes to avoid disruption
Involve the functional manager in line with organisational procedures, documenting what has been tried
quiz.x: Once the PM's own options are exhausted, involve the functional manager and HR process with documentation. Removal is a later decision; doing the work yourself is not leadership.

modules.d: Identifying, analysing and engaging stakeholders; communication planning; negotiation and shared understanding.
modules.body:
Stakeholders decide whether projects succeed

Projects rarely fail for purely technical reasons. They fail because a stakeholder was missed, misunderstood, or disengaged until too late. Stakeholder engagement is therefore continuous: identify early and repeatedly, analyse interests and influence, plan engagement strategies, engage through communication and relationship, and monitor whether engagement levels are moving where they need to be.

Identifying stakeholders — early and often

Start in initiating, from the charter, business case, agreements and organisational charts, and continue throughout the project, because new stakeholders emerge as scope, phases and environments change. A regulator, a union representative, or a community group discovered in execution can force costly rework. The stakeholder register records each stakeholder's role, interests, expectations, influence, and current and desired engagement. On the exam, discovering a new stakeholder late usually triggers: add them to the register, analyse them, update the engagement and communication plans — not ignore them because the plan is baselined.

Analysing stakeholders

The power/interest grid is the most-tested tool: high power, high interest — manage closely; high power, low interest — keep satisfied; low power, high interest — keep informed; low power, low interest — monitor. Variants use influence and impact. The salience model classifies stakeholders by power, urgency and legitimacy. The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix records each stakeholder's current (C) and desired (D) engagement across five levels: unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading. The gap between C and D is what your engagement plan must close.

Pattern to remember: a powerful stakeholder who is resistant is your highest-priority engagement risk. The best first action is usually a direct conversation to understand their concerns — not escalation, and not pressing ahead and hoping they come around.

Communication management

The communications management plan specifies what information is shared, with whom, how often, through which channel, in what format, and who is responsible. It is tailored from stakeholder analysis: executives want concise outcomes and decisions needed; teams want detail and context; regulators want evidence. Communication methods fall into three types: interactive (meetings, calls — best for complex or sensitive matters), push (emails, reports — sent to specific recipients), and pull (portals, wikis — recipients access when needed, good for large audiences).

The number of communication channels grows quickly with team size: n(n−1)/2. A team of 10 has 45 channels; adding 5 people makes 15 people and 105 channels — 60 more. This is why growing teams need more structure, not less.

Effective communication also depends on the sender-receiver model: the sender encodes and confirms understanding; the receiver decodes and acknowledges; noise — language, culture, distance, emotion — distorts the message. When a stakeholder "misunderstood" a report, the exam often points to tailoring the message and confirming understanding, not simply resending it.

Information radiators and transparency in agile

Agile teams favour highly visible, low-ceremony communication: task boards, burndown or burnup charts, and cumulative flow diagrams displayed where stakeholders can see them. Sprint reviews invite stakeholders to inspect working increments and give feedback — the most powerful communication tool in agile, because stakeholders see the product rather than read about it.

Negotiation and building shared understanding

Negotiation in projects — with vendors, functional managers, sponsors and customers — should aim for win-win outcomes that preserve relationships for the long term. Principled negotiation separates people from the problem, focuses on interests rather than positions, generates options for mutual gain, and uses objective criteria. Know your BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) before you begin; it tells you when to walk away.

Building shared understanding means aligning stakeholders on the vision, success criteria and trade-offs. Tools include kickoff meetings, product vision statements, definitions of done, acceptance criteria, prototypes and demonstrations. When two stakeholders want contradictory things, the PM brings them together, clarifies each underlying interest, ties the discussion to the business case, and, if they still cannot agree, escalates to the sponsor or governance body with a clear analysis — the PM does not secretly pick a winner.

Managing expectations

Most stakeholder dissatisfaction comes from a mismatch between expectation and reality, not from the reality itself. Proactive practices — honest early forecasts, visible risks, early demonstration of increments, and prompt notice of variance with options — prevent the "surprise" that destroys trust. The PMI mindset is unambiguous: never hide bad news. Report status truthfully, early, with a plan.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a stakeholder-analysis coach. I will describe a project. Help me build a stakeholder register with power/interest classification, current vs desired engagement levels (unaware/resistant/neutral/supportive/leading), and a tailored engagement action and communication method for each. Then challenge me with 3 situations where a key stakeholder's engagement drops, and grade my responses.

📚 Glossary

  • Stakeholder register: the living record of stakeholders and their characteristics.
  • Engagement assessment matrix: current versus desired engagement per stakeholder.
  • Communication channels: n(n−1)/2 possible paths between n people.
  • Push / pull / interactive: the three communication method types.
  • BATNA: your best alternative if the negotiation fails.
  • Information radiator: a highly visible display of project status.

📖 References

  • Fisher, R., Ury, W. & Patton, B. Getting to Yes.
  • Mitchell, Agle & Wood (1997). Toward a theory of stakeholder identification and salience. Academy of Management Review.
  • PMI, PMBOK® Guide — Stakeholder performance domain.

quiz.q: During execution, the PM learns that a regional environmental authority must approve part of the site works. This authority was not identified during planning. What should the PM do FIRST?
opts: Submit a change request to add the approval activity to the schedule
Add the authority to the stakeholder register and analyse its requirements and influence
Ask the sponsor to contact the authority at an executive level
Continue works on other parts of the site while waiting for contact
quiz.x: A newly identified stakeholder is first recorded and analysed. Change requests and engagement actions follow once their requirements and impact are understood.

quiz.q: A project team grows from 8 to 12 members. How many additional communication channels have been created?
quiz.x: 8 people: 8×7/2 = 28. 12 people: 12×11/2 = 66. The increase is 66 − 28 = 38.

quiz.q: A senior executive with significant budget authority has little interest in the project's day-to-day progress. Which strategy is MOST appropriate?
opts: Monitor with minimal effort
Manage closely with weekly detailed reports
Keep satisfied with concise updates focused on their concerns
Keep informed through the project portal
quiz.x: High power, low interest falls in the 'keep satisfied' quadrant: meet their needs efficiently without burdening them with detail.

quiz.q: The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix shows the finance director as 'resistant' with a desired level of 'supportive'. What is the BEST next step?
opts: Remove dependencies on the finance department from the plan
Increase the frequency of status reports sent to the director
Escalate to the sponsor to secure the director's cooperation
Meet the finance director to understand the concerns driving resistance
quiz.x: Closing an engagement gap starts with understanding the stakeholder's interests and concerns. Escalation or more push communication does not address the cause.

quiz.q: A company-wide policy change affects 2,000 employees who need to read the details at their convenience. Which communication method is MOST suitable?
opts: Interactive — hold sessions with each department
Push — email the full document to every employee
Interactive — a single town hall for all employees
Pull — publish on the intranet with a notification pointing to it
quiz.x: Large audiences who need access at their own pace are best served by pull communication, with a brief notification so they know where to look.

quiz.q: Two influential stakeholders demand conflicting features for the same release, and neither will compromise. The PM has already met each separately. What should the PM do NEXT?
opts: Choose the feature that best fits the PM's view of the business case
Include both features and request additional budget
Bring both stakeholders together to evaluate the options against the business case, escalating to the sponsor if they cannot agree
Defer both features to a later release to avoid conflict
quiz.x: The PM facilitates a joint decision tied to objective criteria and escalates to governance only if needed. Picking a side or quietly deferring removes the decision from those who own it.

quiz.q: A sponsor states that the monthly report 'doesn't tell me what I need to know'. What is the BEST response?
opts: Send the report more frequently so the sponsor sees more data
Meet the sponsor to clarify their information needs and update the communications plan
Add every available metric to the report
Delegate reporting to the PMO to ensure consistency
quiz.x: Communication is tailored to stakeholder needs. Clarifying requirements and updating the plan fixes the cause; more data or frequency does not.

quiz.q: Before negotiating with a vendor, a PM identifies that a second qualified vendor could deliver for 8% more. What does this represent?
opts: The PM's BATNA
The zone of possible agreement
The contingency reserve for procurement
The vendor's reservation price
quiz.x: The best alternative if the negotiation fails is the BATNA; it defines when walking away is better than agreeing.

quiz.q: The project is forecast to miss a milestone by three weeks. The sponsor is travelling and the next steering meeting is in a month. What should the PM do?
opts: Recover the delay quietly through overtime before reporting
Inform the sponsor promptly with the forecast, causes and recovery options
Report the milestone as at risk without specifics until there is certainty
Wait for the steering meeting so the update can be presented formally
quiz.x: Bad news is reported early and honestly, with analysis and options. Delaying or softening status violates honesty and removes the sponsor's chance to act.

quiz.q: On an agile project, stakeholders complain they never know what the team is building. Which action BEST addresses this?
opts: Ask the product owner to filter all stakeholder questions
Require the team to produce documentation for each feature
Send a detailed weekly written status report to all stakeholders
Invite stakeholders to sprint reviews and make the product backlog and board visible
quiz.x: Agile transparency relies on inspecting working increments and visible information radiators, which build shared understanding better than reports.

modules.t: Process I — Scope, Schedule & Cost (with Earned Value)
modules.d: Predictive planning, critical path, estimating, budgets and earned value management.
modules.body:
The predictive planning chain

In predictive delivery, planning flows in a dependable order: collect requirements → define scope → create the work breakdown structure (WBS) → define and sequence activities → estimate durations and costs → develop the schedule and budget → baseline. Each step uses the previous one's outputs, which is why the exam punishes answers that skip steps (for example, estimating cost before the WBS exists).

Scope: requirements, WBS and validation

Requirements are elicited through interviews, workshops, focus groups, prototypes and observation, and traced in a requirements traceability matrix that links each requirement to its business objective, deliverable and test. The scope statement describes deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions, constraints and assumptions. The WBS decomposes the total scope into deliverable-oriented components; the lowest level is the work package, which can be reliably estimated, assigned and controlled. The 100% rule applies: the WBS contains all the work and only the work. The WBS dictionary describes each element. Together — scope statement, WBS and dictionary — they form the scope baseline.

Two control activities are often confused. Control quality checks deliverables are correct against requirements (internal, by the team). Validate scope is the customer or sponsor formally accepting completed deliverables. Quality control generally happens first; validation follows. Scope creep — uncontrolled additions — is prevented through change control. Gold plating — the team adding extras nobody asked for — is also wrong, even if well-intended, because it adds unapproved cost and risk.

Schedule: dependencies and the critical path

Activities are linked by dependencies: finish-to-start (most common), start-to-start, finish-to-finish, start-to-finish. Dependencies may be mandatory (inherent in the work), discretionary (preferred practice), or external (outside the project's control). Leads accelerate a successor; lags delay it.

The critical path is the longest path through the network and determines the shortest possible project duration; activities on it have zero total float. Total float is how long an activity can slip without delaying the project; free float is how long without delaying the next activity. Calculate with a forward pass (earliest start/finish) and backward pass (latest start/finish); float = LS − ES. A project can have more than one critical path, which increases schedule risk.

Compressing the schedule

Crashing adds resources to critical-path activities to shorten them, increasing cost — choose the activities with the lowest cost per unit of time saved. Fast tracking performs activities in parallel that were planned sequentially, increasing risk and potential rework. Compression only helps on the critical path; crashing a non-critical activity wastes money. Resource levelling adjusts the schedule to resource limits and may lengthen the critical path; resource smoothing works within float without changing the end date.

Estimating

Analogous estimating uses a similar past project — fast, less accurate, useful early. Parametric uses a statistical relationship (cost per square metre, hours per unit) — accurate if the model is sound. Bottom-up aggregates work-package estimates — most accurate, most effort. Three-point estimating uses optimistic (O), most likely (M) and pessimistic (P): triangular = (O+M+P)/3; beta/PERT = (O+4M+P)/6, with standard deviation ≈ (P−O)/6. Estimates should be refined as information improves — progressive elaboration — moving from rough order of magnitude (often −25% to +75%) toward definitive estimates.

Budget and reserves

Work-package costs plus contingency reserves (for identified risks — "known-unknowns", controlled by the PM) form the cost baseline. Adding management reserve (for unidentified risks — "unknown-unknowns", controlled by management) gives the total project budget. Using management reserve typically requires a change request because it alters the baseline.

Earned value management

EVM integrates scope, schedule and cost into objective performance measures.

  • PV (planned value): budgeted cost of work scheduled to date. EV (earned value): budgeted cost of work actually completed. AC (actual cost): what the completed work really cost. BAC: total budget.
  • CV = EV − AC (negative = over budget). SV = EV − PV (negative = behind schedule).
  • CPI = EV / AC (below 1 = over budget). SPI = EV / PV (below 1 = behind).
  • EAC = BAC / CPI when current cost performance is expected to continue. Other forms: AC + (BAC − EV) when future work will be at budgeted rate; AC + (BAC − EV)/(CPI × SPI) when both indices affect the remainder.
  • ETC = EAC − AC; VAC = BAC − EAC.
  • TCPI = (BAC − EV) / (BAC − AC): the cost efficiency required on remaining work to finish on budget. Above 1 means harder.
Worked example. BAC = $200,000. At month 4, PV = $100,000, EV = $80,000, AC = $100,000. CV = −$20,000; SV = −$20,000; CPI = 0.80; SPI = 0.80. EAC = 200,000 / 0.8 = $250,000; VAC = −$50,000; ETC = $150,000. TCPI = 120,000 / 100,000 = 1.20 — the team would need to be 20% more efficient than plan on all remaining work to finish on budget, which is rarely realistic. The professional response is to analyse the causes, prepare recovery options and a realistic forecast, and communicate it — not to promise a TCPI of 1.2.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are an EVM drill coach. Give me 6 progressively harder earned value scenarios with BAC, PV, EV and AC. For each, ask me to compute CV, SV, CPI, SPI, EAC, ETC, VAC and TCPI, interpret the project's health in one sentence, and recommend the PM's next action. Check my numbers and reasoning, and show your working for any I get wrong.

📚 Glossary

  • Work package: lowest WBS level, estimable and assignable.
  • Scope baseline: scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary.
  • Critical path: longest path; zero total float.
  • Crashing / fast tracking: compressing with resources / with parallel work.
  • Contingency vs management reserve: identified risks (PM) vs unidentified risks (management).
  • TCPI: efficiency needed on remaining work to meet a target.

📖 References

  • PMI, Practice Standard for Earned Value Management.
  • PMI, Practice Standard for Work Breakdown Structures.
  • PMI, Process Groups: A Practice Guide.

quiz.q: BAC = $500,000, EV = $300,000, AC = $350,000. Assuming current cost performance continues, what is the EAC?
quiz.x: CPI = 300/350 = 0.857. EAC = 500,000 / 0.857 ≈ $583,333. $550,000 is AC + (BAC − EV), which assumes future work at the budgeted rate.

quiz.q: A project has CPI 1.10 and SPI 0.85. Which interpretation is MOST accurate?
opts: Under budget and behind schedule
Under budget and ahead of schedule
Over budget and ahead of schedule
Over budget and behind schedule
quiz.x: CPI above 1 means cost efficiency is better than planned; SPI below 1 means less work was completed than scheduled.

quiz.q: To shorten the schedule, a PM adds two engineers to an activity with 6 days of total float. What is the MOST likely result?
opts: The project end date moves earlier by the time saved
Schedule risk decreases on the critical path
Cost increases without shortening the project
The critical path shifts to this activity
quiz.x: Crashing only shortens the project when applied to critical-path activities. An activity with float is not driving the end date.

quiz.q: The customer refuses to accept a deliverable that passed all internal quality checks, saying it does not meet their needs. Which process gap is MOST likely?
opts: Management reserve was insufficient
Control quality was skipped
The WBS violated the 100% rule
Requirements or acceptance criteria were not adequately defined and agreed
quiz.x: Passing quality control but failing validation usually indicates the requirements or acceptance criteria did not reflect the customer's real needs.

quiz.q: A developer adds an extra reporting dashboard the customer did not request, believing it will impress them. How should the PM view this?
opts: As positive initiative that increases customer value
As gold plating that adds unapproved scope, cost and risk
As acceptable if completed within the existing budget
As scope creep caused by the customer
quiz.x: Adding unrequested features is gold plating. Even within budget it introduces risk, testing effort and unapproved scope.

quiz.q: An activity has O = 4 days, M = 7 days, P = 16 days. What is the PERT (beta) estimate?
opts: 8.0 days
8.5 days
9.0 days
7.0 days
quiz.x: (4 + 4×7 + 16) / 6 = 48 / 6 = 8.0 days. The triangular average would be 9.0.

quiz.q: An identified risk occurs, and its response costs are drawn from the risk-related reserve within the cost baseline. Which reserve was used?
opts: Project buffer in the critical chain
Management reserve
Schedule reserve held by the sponsor
Contingency reserve
quiz.x: Contingency reserves cover identified risks and sit within the cost baseline. Management reserve covers unidentified risks and sits outside it.

quiz.q: With BAC = $200,000, EV = $120,000 and AC = $140,000, what is the TCPI to finish on the original budget, and what does it suggest?
opts: 0.75 — the project can afford to be less efficient
0.86 — performance is acceptable
1.33 — finishing on budget will require significantly better efficiency
1.17 — the project is on track
quiz.x: TCPI = (200 − 120) / (200 − 140) = 80 / 60 = 1.33. A value well above the current CPI (0.86) signals the original budget is unlikely without intervention.

quiz.q: Activities B and C were planned in sequence; the PM decides to run them in parallel to recover two weeks. What risk has MOST increased?
opts: Management reserve consumption
Rework due to overlapping work
Loss of float on non-critical activities
Cost of additional resources
quiz.x: Fast tracking overlaps work and increases the risk of rework. Crashing is the technique that primarily adds cost.

quiz.q: Early in initiating, the sponsor asks for a cost estimate for the business case. Detailed requirements do not yet exist. Which estimating approach is MOST appropriate?
opts: Analogous estimating using similar past projects
Bottom-up estimating from work packages
Earned value forecasting
A definitive estimate based on vendor quotes
quiz.x: With little detail available, analogous estimating gives a fast rough-order-of-magnitude figure. Bottom-up requires a WBS that does not yet exist.

modules.d: Agile values, Scrum and Kanban mechanics, estimation, metrics, and tailoring hybrid approaches.
modules.body:
Why roughly half the exam is agile or hybrid

Modern projects increasingly face uncertain requirements, fast-changing markets and technology that is learned by building. Adaptive approaches handle that uncertainty by delivering in short cycles, inspecting real results, and adapting. The exam does not ask whether agile is "better"; it asks whether you can choose and tailor the right approach and behave correctly inside it.

The values and principles that decide answers

The Agile Manifesto values individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan — while still valuing the items on the right. Its twelve principles stress early and continuous delivery of value, welcoming changing requirements, frequent delivery, daily business–developer collaboration, motivated and trusted individuals, face-to-face conversation, working product as the primary measure of progress, sustainable pace, technical excellence, simplicity, self-organising teams, and regular reflection. When an agile question has two plausible answers, the one closer to these principles usually wins.

Scrum mechanics

Scrum has three accountabilities. The product owner maximises value: owns and orders the product backlog, writes or clarifies items, and accepts or rejects increments. The developers create the increment, own the sprint backlog and decide how to do the work. The scrum master is a servant leader who coaches the team and organisation in Scrum, facilitates events on request, and removes impediments. In a hybrid organisation the PM often performs a role close to scrum master plus broader coordination.

Events: the sprint (fixed timebox, typically 1–4 weeks), sprint planning (what and how), the daily scrum (15 minutes, developers inspect progress toward the sprint goal — not a status report to the PM), the sprint review (inspect the increment with stakeholders, adapt the backlog), and the retrospective (inspect how the team works, choose improvements). Artefacts: product backlog, sprint backlog and the increment, each with a commitment — the product goal, the sprint goal and the definition of done.

High-frequency traps. Mid-sprint, a stakeholder asks the team for a new feature → direct them to the product owner, who adds it to the product backlog; the sprint goal is protected. The team cannot finish a story → it returns to the backlog; it is not partially counted. The daily scrum runs long with problem-solving → take detailed discussions offline after the meeting.

Kanban and flow

Kanban visualises work on a board, limits work in progress (WIP), manages flow, makes policies explicit, and improves continuously. WIP limits create a "pull" system: new work starts only when capacity frees up, exposing bottlenecks. Key metrics are lead time (request to delivery), cycle time (work started to delivered) and throughput. A cumulative flow diagram shows bands widening where work is accumulating — a bottleneck signal. Little's Law links them: average cycle time ≈ WIP ÷ throughput, so reducing WIP is the fastest way to shorten cycle time.

Estimating and planning adaptively

Agile teams often estimate relative size in story points using techniques such as planning poker or affinity estimating. Velocity — points completed per iteration — is used by that team to forecast; it must not be compared across teams or used as a productivity target, because points are team-specific and gaming them destroys their forecasting value. Release planning projects velocity ranges against the ordered backlog. User stories follow INVEST (independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable) with clear acceptance criteria. A spike is a timeboxed research story to reduce uncertainty before estimating. An MVP delivers the smallest product that tests the key value hypothesis with real users.

Metrics and transparency

Burndown charts show remaining work against time; burnup charts show completed work and total scope separately, so scope changes are visible. A flat burndown mid-sprint signals blocked work — the response is to identify impediments, not to pressure the team. Agile progress is measured by working, accepted increments — not by percent-complete estimates.

Choosing and tailoring the approach

Choose adaptive when requirements are uncertain, feedback is cheap, and value can be delivered incrementally. Choose predictive when requirements are stable, regulation demands upfront design, or the work cannot be usefully split (building a bridge foundation). Hybrid combines them: for example, predictive procurement and infrastructure with agile software development, or a phase-gated governance model with iterative delivery inside phases. Tailoring considers organisational culture, team experience, regulatory constraints, risk, and stakeholder expectations. Transitioning an organisation to agile is change management: start with pilot teams, train, coach, adapt governance and metrics, and expect resistance.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are an agile coach simulating a hybrid project. Run me through a 3-sprint scenario: each sprint, give me the backlog, team velocity, a mid-sprint disruption and one stakeholder request. Ask what I do as PM/scrum master. Score me against Scrum Guide rules and Agile Manifesto principles, and show me the burnup chart data after each sprint.

📚 Glossary

  • Definition of done: shared quality standard every increment must meet.
  • Velocity: a team's completed points per iteration, for its own forecasting.
  • WIP limit: cap on items in a workflow stage.
  • Cycle time / lead time: start-to-done / request-to-done.
  • Spike: timeboxed exploration to reduce uncertainty.
  • MVP: minimum viable product that tests the core value hypothesis.

📖 References

  • Schwaber, K. & Sutherland, J. The Scrum Guide (2020).
  • Beck, K. et al. (2001). Manifesto for Agile Software Development.
  • Anderson, D. Kanban: Successful Evolutionary Change.
  • PMI, Agile Practice Guide.

quiz.q: Midway through a sprint, a senior manager asks a developer directly to add an urgent feature. What should the developer do?
opts: Refer the manager to the product owner so the request can be prioritised in the product backlog
Complete the feature during overtime to protect the sprint goal
Ask the scrum master to approve adding the feature
Add the feature to the sprint backlog because the request is urgent
quiz.x: Work enters through the product owner, who orders the product backlog. The sprint goal is protected; nobody outside the team adds work directly mid-sprint.

quiz.q: A department head wants to rank three agile teams by velocity to award a bonus. What is the BEST response from the PM?
opts: Agree, since velocity is the standard agile productivity metric
Suggest ranking teams by number of stories completed instead
Agree, but normalise each team's velocity by team size first
Explain that story points are team-relative and velocity is a forecasting tool, and propose outcome-based measures
quiz.x: Velocity is not comparable across teams and becomes gamed when used as a target. Value delivered and outcomes are better measures.

quiz.q: A cumulative flow diagram shows the 'Testing' band steadily widening while 'Done' grows slowly. What is the BEST response?
opts: Remove testing from the definition of done for this release
Recognise a bottleneck in testing and work with the team to address it, for example with a WIP limit and swarming
Extend the iteration length to allow more testing time
Add more developers to increase throughput
quiz.x: A widening band signals accumulation at that stage. Limiting WIP and helping the constraint improves flow; adding upstream capacity worsens it, and weakening done harms quality.

quiz.q: At the end of a sprint, a story is 90% complete but does not meet the definition of done. How should it be handled?
opts: Mark it done and create a follow-up story for the remaining work
Count 90% of its points toward velocity
Return it to the product backlog for the product owner to reprioritise
Extend the sprint by two days to finish it
quiz.x: Incomplete work is not done and is not partially credited. It returns to the product backlog; the sprint timebox is fixed.

quiz.q: The team cannot estimate a story because it depends on an unfamiliar third-party API. What should they do?
opts: Ask the product owner to remove the story
Create a timeboxed spike to investigate before estimating
Assign the maximum story point value to cover uncertainty
Estimate using the average of the team's other stories
quiz.x: Spikes reduce uncertainty to make estimation possible. Inflating estimates hides the uncertainty rather than resolving it.

quiz.q: A team averages 5 items in progress and completes 2 items per day. Using Little's Law, what is the approximate average cycle time?
opts: 2.5 days
10 days
7 days
0.4 days
quiz.x: Cycle time ≈ WIP ÷ throughput = 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 days.

quiz.q: A government client requires a fixed, detailed design approved before construction of a data centre, but the custom monitoring software is expected to evolve with user feedback. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
opts: Fully predictive for both components to satisfy the client
Fully agile for both components to maximise flexibility
Hybrid — predictive for the facility and adaptive for the software
Kanban for the facility and Scrum for the software
quiz.x: Tailoring matches the approach to each component: stable, regulated physical work suits predictive; evolving software suits adaptive.

quiz.q: During the daily scrum, two developers begin a detailed technical debate that will clearly take 20 minutes. What should the scrum master do?
opts: Resolve the technical question so the meeting can proceed
Cancel the rest of the daily scrum
Let the debate continue since collaboration is valuable
Suggest they continue after the daily scrum with anyone needed
quiz.x: The daily scrum stays focused and timeboxed; detailed problem-solving happens immediately afterward with the relevant people.

quiz.q: Midway through the sprint, the burndown chart has been flat for three days. What should the PM/scrum master do FIRST?
opts: Report the sprint as failed to stakeholders
Ask the team to work overtime to catch up
Work with the team to identify what is blocking progress
Remove lower-priority stories from the sprint immediately
quiz.x: A flat burndown indicates work is stuck. Understanding the impediment precedes any scope negotiation, and pressure does not remove blockers.

quiz.q: Who has final authority to accept or reject that a product backlog item meets stakeholder needs in Scrum?
opts: The project sponsor
The scrum master
The developers, via the definition of done
The product owner
quiz.x: The product owner is accountable for value and accepts work against acceptance criteria. The definition of done covers quality, not whether the item delivers the intended value.

modules.t: Process III — Risk, Quality, Procurement & Change Control
modules.d: Managing uncertainty, building quality in, contracting wisely, and controlling change.
modules.body:
Risk management: uncertainty in both directions

A risk is an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on objectives. Threats and opportunities are both risks — the exam tests opportunity responses as often as threat responses. The cycle: plan risk management (methodology, roles, risk appetite and thresholds), identify risks (brainstorming, checklists, assumption analysis, SWOT, expert judgement), perform qualitative analysis (probability and impact matrix, urgency), perform quantitative analysis where justified (Monte Carlo simulation, decision trees, expected monetary value), plan responses, implement responses, and monitor.

The risk register records each risk, its owner, triggers, analysis and responses. The risk owner is accountable for monitoring and executing the response — not necessarily the PM. A trigger is a warning sign that a risk is about to occur.

Response strategies

  • Threats: Escalate (outside the project's authority), Avoid (eliminate the cause, e.g. change the plan), Transfer (shift impact to a third party — insurance, fixed-price contracts, warranties), Mitigate (reduce probability or impact — prototypes, redundancy, testing), Accept (active: set aside contingency; passive: deal with it if it happens).
  • Opportunities: Escalate, Exploit (make it certain — assign your best people), Share (partner with a party better able to capture it), Enhance (increase probability or impact), Accept.

Responses can create secondary risks (new risks from the response) and leave residual risks (what remains after the response). A fallback plan is used if the primary response fails; a workaround is an unplanned response to an unidentified risk that occurred.

Expected monetary value and decision trees

EMV = probability × impact, with threats negative and opportunities positive. A risk with a 30% chance of a $50,000 loss has an EMV of −$15,000. Decision trees compare options by summing each branch's EMV plus its cost: choose the path with the best expected value. Exam calculations are simple; the trap is sign errors and forgetting the decision's own cost.

Risk vs issue. A risk has not happened; an issue has. When a risk materialises, implement the planned response, update the issue log and risk register, and assess for further impacts. When something happens that was never identified, create a workaround, log the issue, and then ask why risk identification missed it.

Quality: prevention over inspection

Quality is the degree to which characteristics fulfil requirements; grade is a category of features. Low grade can be acceptable; low quality never is. The modern principle — from Deming and Crosby — is that quality is planned and built in, not inspected in. The cost of quality divides into cost of conformance (prevention: training, standards, design reviews; appraisal: testing, inspections) and cost of non-conformance (internal failures: rework, scrap; external failures: warranty, returns, reputation). Prevention is cheapest; external failure is most expensive.

Manage quality (quality assurance) audits processes to make sure they are followed and improved. Control quality inspects and measures deliverables. Key tools: control charts (process stability; a point outside control limits, or the rule of seven — seven consecutive points on one side of the mean — signals an assignable cause to investigate), Pareto charts (80/20 — focus on the few causes producing most defects), cause-and-effect / Ishikawa diagrams (root causes), histograms, scatter diagrams, and checklists. Statistical sampling inspects a portion when testing everything is costly or destructive.

Procurement and contracts

The make-or-buy analysis decides whether to procure. Procurement documents (RFI for information, RFQ for price on defined needs, RFP for proposed solutions) and source selection criteria are prepared before bidders respond. Contract types shift risk differently:

  • Firm fixed price (FFP) — lowest risk to buyer; seller bears cost overruns; needs well-defined scope.
  • Fixed price incentive fee (FPIF) and fixed price with economic price adjustment (FP-EPA) — shared incentives; adjustments for inflation or commodity prices on long contracts.
  • Cost plus fixed fee (CPFF), cost plus incentive fee (CPIF), cost plus award fee (CPAF) — buyer bears cost risk; used when scope is uncertain.
  • Time and materials (T&M) — hybrid; good for small or staff-augmentation work; buyer should cap with a not-to-exceed amount.

Once signed, the contract governs. Changes to a contract must go through the contract's change process and be approved by those with authority — usually the procurement or contracting officer, not the PM. Claims and disputes are preferably resolved through negotiation; alternative dispute resolution follows; litigation is last. Procurement closure includes verifying deliverables, settling claims and archiving records.

Integrated change control

Every change to baselines follows one path: identify the change, document the request, analyse the impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk and resources, submit to the change control board or authorised decision-maker, decide, update plans and baselines if approved, communicate, and implement. The PM never implements an unapproved change, even a small or free one, and never refuses to accept a change request — any stakeholder can submit one. In agile, change is handled by the product owner reordering the backlog; baselines are lighter, but governance still applies to cost, contracts and major direction.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a PMP risk and change-control examiner. Give me 6 scenarios mixing threats, opportunities, materialised risks, unidentified issues, contract changes and change requests. For each, ask for the correct response strategy or next step. After I answer, explain the correct one, name the process involved, and calculate EMV or decision-tree values where relevant.

📚 Glossary

  • Risk owner: person accountable for monitoring and responding to a specific risk.
  • Secondary / residual risk: new risk from a response / risk remaining after it.
  • EMV: probability × impact.
  • Cost of quality: conformance (prevention, appraisal) + non-conformance (failures).
  • Rule of seven: seven consecutive points on one side of the mean signal a non-random cause.
  • CCB: change control board.

📖 References

  • PMI, The Standard for Risk Management in Portfolios, Programs, and Projects.
  • Deming, W. E. Out of the Crisis; Crosby, P. Quality Is Free.
  • PMI, PMBOK® Guide — Uncertainty and Delivery performance domains.

quiz.q: A new technology could cut testing time by 30% if it works. The team's best specialist is reassigned to the project to make sure it is successfully adopted. Which response strategy is this?
opts: Mitigate
Exploit
Enhance
Share
quiz.x: Exploit seeks to make an opportunity certain, often by assigning top resources. Enhance increases probability or impact without seeking certainty.

quiz.q: A risk has a 25% probability of causing a $80,000 loss. A mitigation costing $10,000 reduces the probability to 5%. Based on EMV, what should the PM conclude?
opts: Adopt the mitigation because it reduces EMV by $16,000 at a cost of $10,000
Reject the mitigation because it costs $10,000
Adopt the mitigation because it eliminates the risk
Reject the mitigation because the residual EMV is still negative
quiz.x: EMV falls from −$20,000 to −$4,000, a $16,000 improvement for $10,000 — a net expected benefit of $6,000. It reduces, not eliminates, the risk.

quiz.q: An identified risk occurs exactly as described in the register. What should the PM do FIRST?
opts: Implement the planned response through the risk owner
Hold a risk identification workshop
Submit a change request to use management reserve
Create a workaround and inform the sponsor
quiz.x: Planned responses exist for identified risks; the risk owner implements them. Workarounds are for unidentified risks, and management reserve covers unknown-unknowns.

quiz.q: A control chart shows all points within control limits, but the last seven consecutive points are above the mean. What should the PM conclude?
opts: The process is in control and no action is needed
The process may have an assignable cause that should be investigated
The specification limits must be widened
The process should be stopped immediately
quiz.x: The rule of seven signals a non-random pattern even within limits. Investigate the cause; stopping or changing specifications is premature.

quiz.q: Which spending best represents the cost of conformance?
opts: Compensating a customer for a defective release
Reworking a module after failed acceptance tests
Paying warranty claims on delivered units
Training the team on a coding standard and holding design reviews
quiz.x: Prevention (training, design reviews) and appraisal are costs of conformance. Rework, warranty and compensation are costs of non-conformance.

quiz.q: The buyer has a clearly defined scope and wants to minimise its own cost risk. Which contract type is MOST appropriate?
opts: Time and materials
Cost plus fixed fee
Firm fixed price
Cost plus award fee
quiz.x: FFP places cost risk on the seller and works when scope is well defined. Cost-reimbursable and T&M contracts leave more risk with the buyer.

quiz.q: The vendor suggests an improvement that would add a feature at no extra cost, and the team agrees it is beneficial. What should the PM do?
opts: Reject it because the contract scope is fixed
Approve it immediately since it is free and beneficial
Ask the vendor to implement it quietly and document it later
Process it through change control, analysing impacts before a decision
quiz.x: Even free changes affect testing, risk, schedule and contract terms. They follow integrated change control; rejecting outright also skips analysis.

quiz.q: A team identifies dozens of defect types. Which tool BEST helps decide where to focus improvement efforts first?
opts: Pareto chart
Histogram of defect dates
Scatter diagram
Control chart
quiz.x: Pareto ranks causes by frequency or impact, showing the few causes responsible for most defects.

quiz.q: A key supplier insists on changing the delivery terms in the signed contract. Who usually has the authority to approve the change?
opts: The project manager, as the owner of the project schedule
The project team, by consensus
The authorised contracting or procurement officer, through the contract change process
The supplier, if the change does not affect price
quiz.x: Contract changes follow the contract's change clause and require someone with contracting authority. The PM contributes impact analysis.

quiz.q: A fire suppression system is installed to reduce damage if a fire occurs, and insurance is purchased for the remaining exposure. Which pair of strategies is being used?
opts: Exploit and share
Mitigate and transfer
Enhance and transfer
Avoid and accept
quiz.x: Reducing impact is mitigation; shifting financial impact to an insurer is transfer.

modules.t: Business Environment — Value, Compliance & Organisational Change
modules.d: Business cases, benefits realisation, governance, compliance, external change and sustainability.
modules.body:
The project exists for the business, not the other way round

The Business Environment domain tests whether you connect project work to organisational strategy and value. Its tasks include planning and managing project compliance, evaluating and delivering project benefits and value, evaluating and addressing external business environment changes, and supporting organisational change. Increasingly it also covers governance, sustainability and ethical delivery. Expect scenarios where the technically correct move harms value, compliance or the organisation — and the right answer is the one that protects them.

Business case, benefits and value

The business case justifies the investment: problem or opportunity, options considered, recommended solution, costs, benefits, risks, and financial measures. Common measures: NPV (net present value — higher is better; positive means value is created at the required rate of return), IRR (internal rate of return — higher is better), payback period (shorter is better), benefit–cost ratio (above 1 means benefits exceed costs) and ROI. When comparing projects on NPV, the life span is already accounted for — do not pick based on duration. Opportunity cost is the value of the best option not chosen. Sunk costs are already spent and should not influence future decisions.

The benefits management plan defines target benefits, how and when they will be measured, the benefit owner, and how benefits will be sustained after the project closes — many benefits arrive after handover. A project can be delivered on time and on budget and still fail if it does not realise its benefits. During execution, if conditions change so that the business case no longer holds — the market moved, a regulation changed, a competitor launched first — the PM should raise it with the sponsor and governance; continuing to spend on a project that has lost its justification is not professional loyalty, it is waste.

Value in agile. Adaptive delivery maximises value by ordering the backlog by value, releasing increments early, and measuring outcomes. A product owner may stop development once enough value is delivered — the remaining backlog is not a debt that must be paid.

Governance and the PMO

Governance defines decision rights, escalation paths, approval gates and oversight. The project charter authorises the project and the PM's authority; the sponsor champions it, provides resources and makes decisions beyond the PM's authority. PMOs range from supportive (templates, training), to controlling (compliance with methods), to directive (managing projects directly). Portfolio management selects and prioritises projects and programmes to achieve strategy; programme management coordinates related projects to obtain benefits not available individually.

Compliance

Compliance covers legal, regulatory, contractual, safety, data protection, accessibility, environmental and internal policy requirements. The PM's job: identify requirements early (often with legal, compliance and security specialists), classify them, build them into requirements and the definition of done, assign owners, track evidence, audit, and respond to non-compliance immediately. Non-compliance is never a schedule trade-off: a deliverable that violates regulation is not acceptable however much time it saves. When regulations change mid-project, the PM assesses impact and processes the needed changes through change control — usually with urgency.

External business environment

Markets, technology, economics, politics, regulation, and social expectations shift during projects. Good PMs scan the environment, maintain assumption and constraint logs, and periodically ask whether the project's direction still fits. Tools: PESTLE (political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental) and SWOT. Discovered external changes become inputs to risk management, change control or business-case review.

Organisational change management

Projects deliver change, and people adopt change at different speeds. A new system is worthless if nobody uses it. Organisational change management (OCM) prepares, equips and supports people. The ADKAR model frames individual change: Awareness of the need, Desire to participate, Knowledge of how, Ability to perform, Reinforcement to sustain. Kotter's eight steps frame organisational change: urgency, coalition, vision, communication, removing obstacles, short-term wins, consolidating, anchoring in culture. Resistance is expected — the exam's best answer engages resisters to understand concerns, involves them in design, and supports them with training and communication, rather than mandating compliance.

Sustainability and ethics

Modern project leadership includes environmental and social responsibility: considering energy use, waste, local community impact, inclusive design and fair labour in supply chains. When a cheaper option has significant hidden social or environmental costs, the professional response is to surface those trade-offs to decision-makers transparently.

Closing and transition

Closing confirms acceptance of deliverables, transitions products to operations with training and support documentation, closes contracts, releases resources, captures and shares lessons learned (which should actually be collected throughout the project, not only at the end), archives records, and hands benefit tracking to the benefit owner. Even a terminated project must be formally closed and its lessons captured.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a business-environment strategist for PMP prep. Give me 5 scenarios where external change (regulation, market shift, competitor launch, economic shock, new compliance rule) affects a running project. For each, ask what I would do. Then evaluate my response for business-case thinking, governance, compliance and change management, and calculate any NPV, payback or BCR involved.

📚 Glossary

  • Business case: justification of the investment.
  • Benefits management plan: how benefits are defined, measured, owned and sustained.
  • NPV / IRR / BCR / payback: core financial selection measures.
  • Sunk cost: money already spent; irrelevant to future decisions.
  • ADKAR: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement.
  • PESTLE: environmental scanning framework.

📖 References

  • Hiatt, J. ADKAR: A Model for Change (Prosci).
  • Kotter, J. Leading Change.
  • PMI, The Standard for Portfolio Management; Benefits Realization Management: A Practice Guide.

quiz.q: Midway through a project, a competitor launches a product that makes the project's core value proposition largely obsolete. What should the PM do?
opts: Accelerate delivery to reach the market as soon as possible
Reduce scope to cut costs and finish quickly
Continue as planned because the scope is baselined
Raise the impact on the business case with the sponsor for a governance decision
quiz.x: When the business justification is threatened, governance decides whether to continue, pivot or stop. Acting unilaterally either way bypasses the business-case owner.

quiz.q: Project A has an NPV of $120,000 over 5 years; Project B has an NPV of $95,000 over 2 years. Based on NPV alone, which should be selected?
opts: Neither — NPV cannot compare projects of different durations
Project A, because NPV already accounts for time
Project B, because shorter projects carry less risk
Project B, because it delivers value sooner
quiz.x: NPV discounts cash flows over time, so duration is already reflected. Choose the higher NPV.

quiz.q: A project has spent $2 million of a $3 million budget. Revised analysis shows the remaining $1 million will yield benefits worth only $400,000. What is the MOST appropriate consideration?
opts: Finish the project and adjust the benefits targets afterwards
Continue to protect the $2 million already invested
Recognise the $2 million as sunk cost and recommend governance review the project's continuation
Request additional budget to increase benefits
quiz.x: Sunk costs should not drive decisions. Spending $1 million to gain $400,000 destroys value, so governance should reconsider.
