quiz.q: A new data protection regulation takes effect in three months and affects how the system stores personal data. What should the PM do FIRST?
opts: Assess the regulation's impact on the project with compliance specialists
Delay go-live until the regulation is fully in force
Add the requirement to the next release after launch
Ignore it because the requirements were baselined before the regulation
quiz.x: Compliance requirements cannot be deferred or ignored. The first step is impact analysis with experts, followed by change control.

quiz.q: A new system has been deployed, but staff continue using spreadsheets. Training was delivered. According to ADKAR, which element is MOST likely missing?
opts: Awareness of the system's existence
Knowledge
Ability
Desire
quiz.x: Staff know how (training) and know the system exists, but are not choosing to use it — a gap in desire, often addressed by explaining benefits and involving users.

quiz.q: The team can save four weeks by skipping an accessibility requirement mandated by law, and the sponsor is under pressure to launch. What should the PM do?
opts: Ask the sponsor to accept the risk in writing
Skip it and add it in a later release
Explain that legal compliance is mandatory and explore other ways to recover time
Skip it only for internal users
quiz.x: Legal compliance is not a trade-off. The PM protects the organisation and looks for other legitimate schedule options.

quiz.q: When is the BEST time to collect lessons learned?
opts: At project closure, in a dedicated session
Throughout the project, with a final consolidation at closure
Only after a project fails
At each phase gate, as required by the PMO only
quiz.x: Lessons are captured continuously so they can improve the current project and are not forgotten; closure consolidates them.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST describes the PM's role in benefits realisation?
opts: The PM plans for and enables benefits, then transitions measurement to the benefit owner
The PM delivers outputs only; benefits are irrelevant to the project
The PM measures benefits only if the sponsor requests it
The PM is accountable for all benefits after project closure
quiz.x: Many benefits arrive after closure. The PM enables them and hands over tracking to the designated benefit owner.

quiz.q: A PMO provides templates, training and best practices but does not require projects to use them. Which type of PMO is this?
opts: Portfolio
Supportive
Directive
Controlling
quiz.x: A supportive PMO advises and provides resources with low control. Controlling PMOs require compliance; directive PMOs manage projects.

quiz.q: A project is terminated by the sponsor at 60% completion due to a strategy change. What should the PM do?
opts: Follow closing procedures: document status, close contracts, capture lessons and transition any usable deliverables
Complete the current phase before stopping
Release the team immediately and archive nothing, as the project is cancelled
Continue work until the sponsor confirms in writing a second time
quiz.x: Terminated projects still require formal closure to protect the organisation and preserve knowledge.

modules.d: Integrating domains, timing and question tactics, and a readiness protocol for exam day.
modules.body:
Integration: the PM is the one who sees the whole

Integration management is what makes everything else coherent. The PM integrates across knowledge areas, delivery approaches, stakeholders and time: the charter authorises the work, the project management plan integrates subsidiary plans and baselines, direct-and-manage work produces deliverables, monitoring compares performance against plans, integrated change control governs adjustments, and closing finalises everything. On the exam, integration thinking appears whenever one event affects several areas — a scope change that alters schedule, cost, risk, quality and contracts. The correct answer usually considers the whole impact, not one dimension.

The tailored project management plan

The plan is not a document for its own sake; it is the agreed way this project will be run. In predictive projects it contains the scope, schedule and cost baselines and subsidiary plans. In agile projects much of it lives in lightweight artefacts: the product vision, roadmap, backlog, definition of done and working agreements. In hybrid projects the plan explains which parts use which approach and how they integrate. Tailoring is expected — a small internal project does not need the governance of a national infrastructure programme.

Time management on exam day

Know the current timing and break structure from the PMP Handbook. Calculate your pace: if you have roughly 1 minute 15 seconds per question, plan checkpoints (for example, question 60 by minute 75) and stick to them. Take the scheduled breaks; fatigue in the final block costs more marks than the minutes saved. Never leave a question blank — there is no penalty for wrong answers.

A disciplined method for every question

  1. Read the last sentence first. First? Next? Best? Should have done? Choose two?
  2. Identify the context. Predictive, agile or hybrid? Which phase? What has already been done?
  3. Predict the answer before reading the options, using the PMI mindset.
  4. Eliminate two options. Usually one is unethical or bypasses process, and one skips a step.
  5. Compare the final two by asking which one a servant-leader PM following process would do at this moment.
  6. Mark and move if still unsure after about 90 seconds; return later with fresh eyes.
The ten most common distractor patterns. ① Escalate to sponsor before trying anything. ② Implement a change before approval. ③ Fire or replace a person first. ④ Act without analysing impact. ⑤ Ignore a stakeholder or regulation because the plan is baselined. ⑥ Hide or delay bad news. ⑦ Assign tasks in a self-organising team. ⑧ Add work mid-sprint without the product owner. ⑨ Crash a non-critical activity. ⑩ Treat a materialised identified risk with a workaround instead of the planned response.

Handling the question types

Multiple response — the question states how many to select; treat each option as true/false against the scenario. Matching — start with the pairs you are certain of to narrow the rest. Hotspot — read axes and labels carefully (a burnup chart's scope line, a control chart's limits, a power/interest grid quadrant). Calculations — write formulas on your whiteboard at the start, check signs, and sense-check: if CPI is below 1, EAC must exceed BAC.

Your final four weeks

Week −4: full timed mock; analyse by domain and by error type — knowledge gap, misread question, or mindset error. Week −3: targeted remediation of the weakest domain and the top error type; 200+ questions. Week −2: second full mock; formula and framework review; revisit every wrong answer log entry. Week −1: light review only, mixed sets of 30–50, sleep, logistics, ID, test-centre route or online proctoring setup and room check. Do not take a full mock in the final 48 hours.

Readiness criteria

You are ready to book when you consistently score around 75% or higher on two or more full-length mocks from quality sources, no domain is below target in your practice analysis, you can explain the reason for every answer — not just recognise it — and you finish mocks within time with a margin. If you are not there, postponing a week or two is far cheaper than a retake.

After the exam

Your PMP is maintained through the Continuing Certification Requirements System: earn 60 professional development units every three years across Education (Ways of Working, Power Skills, Business Acumen) and Giving Back. Keep a running log from day one. Teaching, mentoring, writing and volunteering all count toward Giving Back — Team21's mentor model gives you a natural path.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a full PMP mock-exam proctor. Give me 30 mixed situational questions across People, Process and Business Environment, roughly half predictive and half agile/hybrid, including 3 calculation items and 2 'choose two' items. Do not reveal answers until I finish. Then score me by domain, classify each error as knowledge gap, misread question, or mindset error, and give a readiness verdict with a 2-week remediation plan.

📚 Glossary

  • Integrated change control: single governed path for all baseline changes.
  • Tailoring: adapting approach, processes and artefacts to context.
  • Mindset error: choosing a plausible action that violates PMI's professional logic.
  • CCR / PDU: continuing certification requirements / professional development units.

📖 References

  • PMI, PMP Certification Handbook and Continuing Certification Requirements Handbook.
  • PMI, PMBOK® Guide — Tailoring section.
  • PMI, Process Groups: A Practice Guide.

quiz.q: A client requests a scope addition. The PM has documented the request. Which sequence BEST reflects integrated change control from here?
opts: Submit for decision, analyse impact if approved, implement
Update the schedule, analyse cost, request client signature
Analyse impact, submit for decision, update plans if approved, communicate, implement
Implement, update baselines, inform the client
quiz.x: Impact analysis precedes the decision; baselines change only after approval; communication and implementation follow.

quiz.q: A candidate's mock analysis shows most wrong answers chose 'escalate to the sponsor' as a first step. What type of error is this primarily?
opts: A calculation error
A knowledge gap about the sponsor's role
A misreading of question length
A mindset error about resolving issues at the lowest appropriate level
quiz.x: Repeatedly escalating first reflects the PMI mindset error of skipping the PM's own analysis and lower-level resolution.

quiz.q: On a calculation question, a candidate gets CPI = 0.9 and EAC lower than BAC. What should they conclude?
opts: The answer is plausible because the project is under budget
There is likely an error, since CPI below 1 implies EAC above BAC when performance continues
The question must be using the TCPI formula
EAC is always lower than BAC on predictive projects
quiz.x: With CPI below 1, EAC = BAC/CPI exceeds BAC. A sense-check catches sign and division errors.

quiz.q: A small internal project with three people and a two-month timeline is required by the PM to produce every document in the organisation's large-programme methodology. What principle is being neglected?
opts: Integration
Benefits realisation
Tailoring
Progressive elaboration
quiz.x: Approach, processes and artefacts should be tailored to the project's size, risk and context.

quiz.q: A candidate has scored 68%, 71% and 70% on three full mocks and their exam date is in five days. What is the MOST prudent action?
opts: Consider rescheduling while remediating the weakest domain and error type
Keep the date because practice exams are usually harder than the real exam
Keep the date and focus on memorising formulas
Take two more full mocks before the exam
quiz.x: Consistent scores below the readiness benchmark suggest risk. Rescheduling with targeted remediation is cheaper than a retake; cramming full mocks just before the exam adds fatigue.

quiz.q: A question asks: 'What should the PM have done to prevent this situation?' The scenario describes a key stakeholder blocking approval late in the project. Which answer is MOST likely correct?
opts: Replaced the stakeholder's representative
Escalated to the sponsor as soon as the block occurred
Added management reserve for stakeholder delays
Identified and engaged the stakeholder early, keeping them involved throughout
quiz.x: 'Should have done' questions point to prevention. Early identification and engagement would have avoided the late surprise.

quiz.q: A hybrid project uses a predictive phase for hardware procurement and Scrum for software. The software team requests a change to a feature. Who should handle it first?
opts: The change control board, since the project has baselines
The PM, who updates the software baseline
The product owner, who reorders the product backlog
The procurement officer, since a contract exists
quiz.x: Within the agile component, feature changes are handled through the product backlog by the product owner, unless they affect contracts, budget or governance thresholds.

quiz.q: Which practice gives the strongest indicator of genuine exam readiness?
opts: Being able to explain why each option is right or wrong on new questions
Recognising most questions from your question bank
Memorising all formulas and process names
Finishing mocks with 40 minutes spare
quiz.x: Explaining the reasoning on unseen questions shows transferable judgement. Recognising repeated questions inflates scores.

quiz.q: During the exam, a candidate has spent three minutes on a question and is down to two plausible options. What is the BEST tactic?
opts: Choose the longer option, as it is usually correct
Select the more likely option, mark it for review, and move on
Keep working until certain, since every question counts
Leave it blank and return at the end
quiz.x: Answer, mark and move protects time for other questions. Blanks score nothing, and option length is not a reliable signal.

quiz.q: A newly certified PMP mentors junior PMs in their organisation for free and wants to count it toward certification maintenance. Into which CCR category does it MOST likely fall?
opts: Education — Ways of Working
It cannot be counted
Education — Business Acumen
Giving Back
quiz.x: Volunteering, mentoring and sharing knowledge typically count toward Giving Back PDUs.
